questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Availability of subjects interesting to me. Destination not too similar to my own culture, and not a place I had been before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The university of Helsinki had assigned 3 tutors to my group of about 20 exchange students. Two of these students were themselves international students, and knew the challenges we could face as non-Finnish people.
The University of Helsinki had arranged introductory presentations and excursions to get all the bureaucracy done. It felt like I was helped most of the way.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Tutors, help with signing up for subjects, help with discovering extra curricular activities, invitations to social events, excursions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used an agency that took a 200€ premium for linking me up with the landlord, and an additional 2% surcharge on the deposit. They were friendly, and the housing I was hooked up with suited my needs. private housing options in Helsinki are expensive, expect similar rents as Copenhagen. However, many of my friends lived in student accommodation, which there is a lot of. I was also offered a student dorm room once I arrived, but I had already made an advance payment with the private accommodation, which was more centrally located, so I stuck with it. So there are cheaper student options.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Try to find a Helsinki student who is themselves going abroad, and rent their room. One of my exchange friends did this, and their flat was the best value for money.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The reason I didn't get student accommodation was that I applied in round two of applications, and dorms were filled up. Helsinki has much more affordable housing available to students, and most of my exchange group lived in student accommodation.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Course registration is messy and confusing. Registering to subjects involves 2 websites, one for searching and one for signing up. On the other hand, the process is infinitely more flexible than UCPH, as you can apply for any number of subjects and then just drop out if you realise you don't want to finnish the course. The credits are only binding once you finnish the exam.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Tutors, this is the only thing that was not described very well by the university in any official place that I found. But the tutors were very helpful, and a full afternoon was dedicated to choosing subjects for the whole semester

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very succesful, and the flexibility of the system also allowed me to change subjects a few weeks in, as I was dissatisfied with certain courses. UCPH can learn from this.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sign up to any and all course sthat sound interesting, and try out 1 or 2 lectures. If it seems to difficult, you don't have time, or it is not interesting to you, just drop the course. You end up with the ideal semester this way. Also consider the possibility of doing the MOOC courses which are fully remote and online. The university has great facilities for studying on campus (club rooms, IT rooms) so you can be social with other students doing the same thing, but decide on your own time and terms when to work on the courses and when to complete them. This way, you make time for social activities and excursions.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Tried some masters courses. If they were too hard I dropped them and did a bachelors course instead

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Physical lectures are similar. emphasis on student participation in tutorials to a greater extent than mine at UCPH (i.e. students working on blackboard, discussing solutions). Helsinki and other Finnish universities make available very high quality online courses which can be worked on and finnished on your own time. These courses offer subjects that a re not taught physically. These are great and I am envious that Finnish students have this option.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: networking technologies, combinatorial optimisations, functional programming I and II, Cyber security intro, topics and project, Finnish for exchange students

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you want to engage with Finnish culture in any meaningful way, the Finnish course for exchange students is very good, because it teaches you spoken Helsinki Finnish. Finland has many local varieties, and no one actually speaks standard language which is what is taught in online courses such as duolingo. I had prepared with duolingo in advance, and I straight up had to unlearn what I had been taught, because it was not useful in everyday situations.
Cyber security is a great online course, very relevant today, and very fun exercises such as snooping cookies, finding secret messages and a project of making an app with flaws from the OWASP top 10 that you then have to fix. 
Combinatorial optimisations is an interesting subject and is taught by a very engaging lecturer, Matti Järvisalo, highly recommend, if you like optimisation problems (Simplex, dual simplex gomory cuts etc)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food is very cheap because student canteens are subsidized by student unions. Denmark can learn from this.
Other prices were generally comparable to Danish prices

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I had a subsidized gym membership. The gyms have saunas. I was member of the comp-sci student association which held parties and other activities. Many clubs for many fields of interest. There is a day "tori" where all the associations are ligned up in stalls outside the main university building in the city centre, and students can meet the associations.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Try at least one "sitsit" which is a traditional Finnish student party. Go to sauna at least once. If in Helsinki, you can go to Sompa Sauna which is a free sauna run by volunteers.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Bring camping and hiking gear and make use of Finlands beautiful nature, They have an abundance of national parks with lean to shelters and open wild huts where park service leaves firewood for visitors. Tampere is the next big town in the region, 2 hrs by train. Very beautiful but slightly smaller city. Home to the worlds oldest public wood fired sauna and a very good and fairly priced food market "kauppahalli". Don't go to turku, not worth the time. it's expensive and hideous. Try to go to Lapland while it is still warm enough to camp out. if you do you can make it a very affordable trip, as train tickets have student discounts, and you save the accommodation by camping out. lapland is great in winter as well. Skiing in Finland is OK, not amazing, but still fun. I enjoyed a day of skiing in Levi.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I didn't adjust before the last month.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join an association, and do activities. Finnish people don't smalltalk. And I don't mean like Danish people don't smalltalk, they do not talk AT ALL. You are WEIRD if you talk to someone you don't know. So lower your expectations and just try to get to know people by doing things together with them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Finnish people don't like talking to strangers whatsoever, even lightheartedly. Finnish people are not comfortable speaking English, and they don't want to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Sauna, sitsit, student associations

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Enjoy nature while it's warm, learn some basic finnish, lower your expectations for interacting with Finns

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look for student discounts, there are many. The only place where you can talk to Finns almost guaranteed is in the sauna. A safe icebreaker is just asking something about the sauna, they love talking about it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Associations, sauna culture

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finnish people

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
